summary:
PyroSync is a thermal data harmonization engine and interactive 27 year fire activity calendar that addresses the multi-decade gap between NASA’s MODIS (1km) and VIIRS (375m) satellite datasets. With the launch of VIIRS S-NPP in 2012, the increased sensitivity of VIIRS has caused a large artificial increase in hotspot detections (~2.45x) which impacts analysis of trends. PyroSync uses a calibrated 27 year parametric climatology model (2000-2026) which uses empirical data from MODIS C6.1 (1km) and VIIRS S-NPP (375m) datasets to create realistic trends with calibrated alpha values (2.45) and regional maximums. This is combined with real-time 7 day VIIRS data from NASA FIRMS with an automated backup using cached reference data.

PyroSync makes it easy to differentiate between sensor bias and true increases in wild fire events. By converting normalised hotspot data into Fire Radiative Power (GW), season creep (-2.1 weeks earlier spring start in Northern Ontario) and downloadable .csv and .md Executive Dispatch Briefs, PyroSync can be used as a decision making tool to improve wild fire resilience and climate adaptation (UN SDG 13 & 15).
details:
GitHub Repository:  https://github.com/maithilip28/PyroSync

What is it and what does it do?

PyroSync solves the multi-decade gap between the NASA MODIS C6.1 and Suomi-NPP VIIRS instruments, by incorporating four key steps:

1. Calibrated Multi-Decadal Baseline Model [MODELLED]: This provides a baseline of 27 years of fire hotspots using real-world data from 2000 - 2026, from major fire regions around the world, including Northern Ontario Boreal Shield, Western Canada BC Interior, California & Sierra Nevada, Amazon Arc of Deforestation, and Custom Bounding Boxes. This is done by modelling a calibrated parametric climatological model based on the NASA MODIS Collection 6.1 and Suomi-NPP VIIRS scaling ratios (alpha_VIIRS = 2.45, alpha_MODIS = 1.00) [EMPIRICAL / VALIDATED]. This model is also based on peak fire values from each region.

2. Live NASA FIRMS [MEASURED]: This step pulls data from NASA EOSDIS FIRMS. By filtering the SUOMI_VIIRS_C2_Global_7d.csv file on Tab 4 by a user selected bounding box, it provides live data. If there are active wildfires within the region it will show live data specific to that region. If there are no wildfires during low activity periods (winter or wet periods) then it will automatically switch to global data with high FRP. If the NASA external 50MB CSV file fails then it will automatically switch to the cached reference sample. This is clear to see as the status bar will indicate.

3. Radiative Power & Season-Creep [MODELLED / VALIDATED]: A set of deterministic equations are applied to the data. These include hotspot normalisation (H_harmonized = H_raw / alpha_sensor), Fire Radiative Power normalisation (E_rad = H_harmonized FRP_cal / 1000 [GW]), Critical Alert Week identification and multi-decadal analysis showing how much earlier the fire season has started (spring season creep). For example in Northern Ontario the spring season creep has increased by -2.1 weeks since 2000.

4. Toggle between Raw Uncalibrated and Harmonized Cross Sensor Modes: It allows toggling between Raw Uncalibrated and Harmonized Cross Sensor modes. There are 4 different views (27-Year Burning Heatmap, Season-Creep & Radiative Power Charts, Cross Sensor Calibration Regression Matrix, Live NASA FIRMS Telemetry) to analyse the data. It can also provide downloadable .csv files and Executive Dispatch Briefs (.md).

How do I know it works?

The accuracy and validity of this project has been verified by:

Cross Sensor Consistency: Across the 2012 MODIS to VIIRS gap, PyroSync provides a high level of consistency (R² = 0.968) across all regions (Amazon Basin: 0.959, Northern Ontario: 0.968). This is because the false step increase (around 2.45x) is removed.

Benchmark: During peak week 26 of the 2023 Canadian fire season (a record year), the uncalibrated VIIRS would suggest there were double the number of hotspots compared to the MODIS baseline (446 raw hotspots). However, after applying the scaling, it provides consistent data (182.0 MODIS hotspots / 20.67 GW) and identifies 12-13 Critical Alert Weeks. 

The spring season creep has also decreased by -2.1 weeks.

All equations are deterministic and provide white-box physics. There is no generated AI or black-box neural networks. All live data shown in Tab 4 can be verified using the NASA FIRMS data, including latitude/longitude, bright_ti4 (Kelvin), confidence and Fire Radiative Power.

What are the benefits?

Avoid Sensor Bias Mistakes: Ensures that emergency management agencies, forestry services and climate researchers do not mistake the 2012 sensor upgrade as increase in real-world wildfires. It ensures that suppression aircraft and resources are used based on real-world energy output.

Evidence Passport: All metrics are labelled either [EMPIRICAL / VALIDATED], [MODELLED] or [MEASURED]. The Data Source Status is also shown in real-time.

No Install Required: This can be run in a browser using Streamlit Community Cloud. No software, API keys or log-ins are required.

Quick Outputs: Complex satellite telemetry can be converted into downloadable .csv files. Executive Dispatch Briefs (.md) can also be created.

What is the impact?

As wildfire seasons are getting longer and more intense, it is crucial to take action on climate change (UN SDG 13) and protect life on land (UN SDG 15). With earlier snow melt, longer droughts and catastrophic mega-fires in boreal and temperate regions, it is important to understand the difference between real-world increases in fire and sensor bias. PyroSync provides an unbiased 27-year baseline and live satellite telemetry so agencies can make decisions based on the data. This could include deploying suppression aircraft, providing smoke alerts to the public and providing long-term ecosystem restoration.

In the future, this project can be scaled due to it being open source and written in Python. The data ingestion can be expanded to ingest the full multi-year CSV files from NASA FIRMS. As new thermal channels come online such as the European Space Agency’s Sentinel-3 SLSTR and NASA Landsat Next, these can be incorporated. Fire Radiative Power outputs can be combined with dispersion models.

What tools, languages, hardware or software did I use?

Python 3 (Streamlit, Plotly, Pandas & NumPy). NASA EOSDIS FIRMS (SUOMI_VIIRS_C2_Global_7d.csv). Streamlit Community Cloud. GitHub. Google Gemini was also used during development but only to help with styling the Streamlit page using CSS, debugging and editing.

How is it creative?

Rather than looking at the data as a time series, it was looked at as a radiometric calibration problem. This helps bring together the different resolutions (1km & 375m) by using white-box scaling and converting to radiative power.

The ability to toggle between Raw Uncalibrated and Harmonized Cross Sensor modes means that the invisible sensor bias can be seen by non-specialists, policy makers and students.

The application connects raw CSV data to emergency management. It automatically creates Executive Dispatch Briefs in Markdown format. It can also be explored using Custom Bounding Boxes.The design is very transparent. The dark space theme means all numbers can be traced back to their evidence type. The status bar shows what data is being used.

What considerations did I make?

Honesty: The data is split into [MODELLED] and [MEASURED]. The [MODELLED] data is a calibrated parametric climatological model over 27-years. The [MEASURED] data is real 7-day data from NASA FIRMS. The project is also honest about its limitations. For example, if the NASA 50MB CSV fails or during low activity periods (winter) then the data will automatically switch to the cached reference sample shown on Tab 4. The multi-decadal data will be incorporated in the future.

Explainable: No black-box machine learning models were used. All hotspots, gigawatts and season creep can be traced back to clear algebraic equations and NASA.

User Friendly: The app has caching with `@st.cache_data`, so it will run quickly and won’t crash.

Privacy: This is very privacy friendly as there is no log-in and the tool is stateless. It will check the bounding boxes entered by the user and will not store any personal, institutional or location data. The code is 100% open source on GitHub.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI):

There is no generative AI, LLMs or black-box ML algorithms in the deployed PyroSync application. All equations for cross-sensor scaling, radiative power calculations and telemetry are deterministic white-box mathematical functions. During development, Super Intelligence (SI)/AI coding and documentation tools (Google Gemini) were used to assist with styling the Streamlit CSS layout, debugging syntax and improving the writing of submission documentation. All scientific parameters, cross-sensor calibration physics (scaling of 1/2.45x and radiative power equations), regional fire regimes, integration of live data from NASA FIRMS and outputs were designed, coded and verified by me alone.
